title: Expectation Damages Lost Profits Certainty
subject: Contracts
subtopic: Expectation damages - lost profits - reasonable certainty
stem: On April 2, Mary signed a one-month lease for Caleb's calibrated CNC cutting bay to launch a custom sign-making service. Caleb breached by locking the bay and refusing Mary access. Mary had not previously operated a sign-making business, but she had already received prepaid work orders for three-quarters of the month's available cutting time, had fixed materials costs under supplier contracts, and offered testimony from an experienced accountant using those contracts and comparable local shop data.

choices.A: Mary may recover lost net profits if the evidence proves them with reasonable certainty.
choices.B: Mary cannot recover lost profits because the sign-making service was a new business.
choices.C: Mary may recover the gross order revenue without subtracting materials costs.
choices.D: Mary may recover only nominal damages because no sign-making job had been completed yet.

rightExplanation: Lost profits are expectation damages. A new business is not automatically barred from recovering them. The claimant must prove net profits with reasonable certainty, not speculation. Mary's prepaid work orders, fixed supplier costs, and accountant testimony based on comparable local shop data can supply a reliable basis for calculating net profit. If that proof satisfies the reasonable-certainty requirement, she may recover those lost net profits caused by Caleb's breach.

wrongExplanations.B: The new-business label is a strong shortcut because untested ventures often lack reliable profit history. Modern doctrine rejects a categorical bar when other evidence proves net profits with reasonable certainty.
wrongExplanations.C: Gross order revenue sounds like the value Mary lost from the breach. Expectation damages for lost profits subtract the costs saved or avoided by not performing.
wrongExplanations.D: No completed jobs makes the business look too speculative. Pre-opening status does not limit damages to nominal damages when reliable evidence supports a net-profit calculation.
